analysis: Examined ClusterService.swift (head lines 1-910). The PR adds a `Listening` struct (ports, interface policy, optional selection) and a `listenerChange` check that replaces the cable-only `cableMove` check. It now also detects a pairing change or unpairing and tears down the responder. `ensureResponder` (lines 387-436) stops the responder on any change, then rebuilds it only if a current pairing and selection exist. Security effect is positive: after unpair or re-pair, the listener stops answering with the stale edge secret instead of continuing to accept the old pairing's connections. Listener identity comes from `ClusterSetupLinkExchange.pairing(store:)` and compares `Pairing.Identity` against `listener.pairing`. A pairing-store read error returns nil, so the old listener stays up; this fail-open on unreadable state is a minor availability choice, and I found no concrete regression. The new `listening` init parameter is internal (not public), defaults to the thunderboltOnly policy and the fixed exchange/control ports, and only test composition can override it, so there is no new external attack surface visible. The `responder` property was widened from private to internal and is used by the control extension (ClusterServiceControl.swift, not supplied); that file's use of `controlCheck` and `listening.controlPort` was not reviewed. The command handlers (serve/stop/approval/batchSetup) are unchanged and still gate on `followsPeer`, the claim term check and the control lock. This area is only loosely tied to the provider threat model (TB-002 and A-008 are not materially touched). Remaining question: whether the unseen ClusterServiceControl.swift applies the same listenerChange semantics to the control responder.
